# Overview {#Initialconsiderations-Overview}

In this Handbook we define alternative data sources as ***data sources
that differ from traditional price collection in how price information
is generated, observed and accessed***.

The use of alternative data sources has the potential to fundamentally
change how consumer price statistics are produced. These include
transaction data such as scanner data, e-invoice data and administrative
transaction data where prices are associated with actual purchases and
typically include information on quantities or expenditures, and
non-transaction data such as web-scraped data and online advertisements
data, where prices reflect posted or offered prices but typically do not
include quantities, expenditures or confirmation that a transaction has
occurred. Both types of data sources offer potential improvements in
coverage, accuracy and efficiency. 

However, before moving to implementation, national statistical offices
(NSOs) are encouraged to take a structured and deliberate approach to
assessing why alternative data sources are being introduced, what role
they are intended to play within the index framework, and how they can
be integrated into existing statistical processes. Early decisions in
these areas can have lasting implications for index design, operational
practices and resource requirements.

This section sets out key considerations relevant during the early
stages of exploration and planning. It is intended to support informed
decision-making and to help NSOs identify the areas that require more
detailed investigation, many of which are addressed in subsequent
chapters of the Handbook.

While this Handbook focuses on the use of alternative data sources in
the production of consumer price statistics, many of the data sources
and processes described are also relevant to [other areas of official
statistics](other-uses-of-alternative-data-beyond-cpi.qmd),
including purchasing power parities, national accounts, business price
indices, and business statistics. Where appropriate, the handbook
highlights considerations that may support broader reuse of data across
statistical domains, while recognising that conceptual requirements and
methodological choices may differ.
